t.big solar furnace@41.3,69.7:
In the foothills of the Tian Shan, about an hour north-east of Tashkent, there is a building that looks as if it belongs in a science fiction film: a huge curved mirror, made of thousands of smaller mirrors, facing a field of tracking mirrors that follow the sun and focus its light onto a single point. This is the Big Solar Furnace near Parkent, built in the Soviet era in the 1980s, and still used for research into materials that can withstand extremely high temperatures.

The facility was designed to study how materials behave at temperatures of several thousand degrees, with applications in the space programme and industry. Its site was chosen for its many sunny days and clean air. Today, it is run by the Uzbek Academy of Sciences and can be visited on guided tours, which explain how the mirrors work and let you walk around the vast concave reflector. It is one of the strangest and most impressive sights in the region.

The road from Tashkent passes through the town of Parkent and climbs into the foothills, with views of the mountains of the Chatkal range ahead. The roads in this area range from decent to badly broken, and traffic in and around Tashkent is heavy and chaotic. In the mountains, the roads are quieter but expect potholes, gravel and livestock. Further on, the road toward Chimgan and the Charvak reservoir is a popular weekend getaway for Tashkent residents, with ski slopes in winter and lakes in summer.

Parkent, about six kilometres away, has basic services, and Chirchiq, a larger industrial town, is a little further. Fuel in Uzbekistan can be tricky: many vehicles run on gas, petrol may be low-octane or in short supply, so fill up wherever good fuel is available. Check the rules for bringing your own motorcycle into the country. Food in Uzbekistan centres on plov, shashlik and fresh bread; the markets are full of fruit in summer, especially melons and grapes. Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, with mild weather and clear views.
t.the chatkal state biosphere nature reser:
East of Tashkent, the land rises steeply into the western ranges of the Tian Shan, and the Chatkal range forms the border with Kyrgyzstan. The Chatkal State Biosphere Reserve, established in the Soviet era, protects a stretch of these mountains, with juniper forests, walnut and wild fruit trees, alpine meadows and rocky peaks. The point at these coordinates lies in the reserve's area between Yangiobod, Parkent and the mining town of Angren.

The reserve is home to rare animals, including the snow leopard, the Tian Shan brown bear, the Siberian ibex and the Menzbier's marmot, a species found only in this region. The forests of wild apple, apricot and walnut are of special interest: Central Asia is the ancestral home of the domestic apple, and these trees are a genetic treasure. Access to the strict reserve itself is limited and usually requires permits, but the surrounding mountains, part of the Ugam-Chatkal National Park, are open to visitors.

The road from Tashkent toward Angren and over the Kamchik pass into the Fergana valley is the main route through these mountains, a major highway climbing to over two thousand metres, with tunnels and checkpoints. It is busy with trucks but scenic. Side roads lead into the valleys and toward villages and summer pastures, often unpaved and rough. Further north, the Chimgan and Charvak area is the most popular weekend escape for Tashkent residents.

Riding in Uzbekistan requires preparation. Fuel supplies can be erratic, petrol may be low-octane, and many vehicles run on gas; carry extra fuel. Check the requirements for bringing your own motorcycle into the country, and expect police checkpoints. Mountain roads can be damaged by landslides and snow, and the Kamchik pass can close in winter.

Yangiobod, about seventeen kilometres away, Parkent and Angren have basic services, and Tashkent, around two hours away, has everything. Food in the mountains is simple: shashlik, plov, bread, fresh fruit and yoghurt. Late spring, when the meadows are full of flowers, and early autumn, when the walnuts ripen, are the best times to visit.
t.rabati malik sardoba@40.1,65.1:
Halfway between Samarkand and Bukhara, the old caravan road crosses a stretch of steppe that is flat, dry and almost empty, and in the eleventh century someone decided that a traveller crossing it deserved a proper stopping place. Rabati Malik, the Rabat of the King, was built in the 1070s by a Karakhanid ruler named Shams al-Mulk Nasr, on one of the main branches of the Silk Road. The caravanserai itself is now mostly collapsed, and what remains is a tall brick entrance portal, ornamented with carved terracotta, standing alone in the plain like the front of a theatre set.

Nearby is the sardoba, and this is the part that explains why anyone could live out here. A sardoba is a domed cistern, built over a pit to catch and store rainwater and the water brought by canal, and in a land with a tough dry summer it was as vital as a well. The domed brick chamber sits low and round, with steps leading down, and its thick walls kept the water cool. The caravans would arrive here at the end of a hard day, the animals would be watered, the merchants would sleep under the arches, and in the morning they would load up and go. It is easy to imagine, because the landscape has changed so little.

The ride here is on straight roads through the desert steppe, with the Nurata mountains a faint line in the north. Navoi, twenty kilometres away, is the nearest large town, and is where you should buy fuel and water. The road itself is good in stretches and rough in others, with trucks and the occasional herd of sheep to dodge, and sandstorms can bring visibility down in minutes. Spring is by far the best season, when the steppe is briefly green and covered in poppies. In summer the heat bounces off the asphalt.

Bring a hat, because there is no shade at the site, and some water. A stop of half an hour is plenty for the portal and the cistern, but the silence is worth lingering over. The Deggaron mosque in the ride title is a short drive away, and the old villages around the Zeravshan river offer shade, tea and fresh bread.
t.kasim sheikh architectural complex@40.1,:
Dabusiya is an ancient settlement on the Zeravshan, the river that rises in the Tajik glaciers, flows past Samarkand and Bukhara, and then dwindles into the sands before reaching the sea. Of the old fortified town, there are now mounds, a few ruined walls and a clear sense of where the river used to run. In its prime, around the sixth century, it lay on the route between the two great oases, and it was famous in the early Islamic period; the geographers write of its markets and of a decisive battle that was fought in the area in the eighth century. The Kasim Sheikh complex in the label belongs to the same shrine tradition as many sites near Navoi: a saint's tomb, a mosque and a small cluster of domes and arches that turned a hill into a pilgrimage place.

It is worth saying what these places mean in Uzbekistan. A Sufi sheikh's grave is not a museum but a living site, where people come to pray, to ask for children or rain, or simply to sit on the shaded platform and talk. Visitors are welcome, but they should dress modestly, take off their shoes at the right place, and keep their voices down. A small donation to the custodian is always appreciated. The tiles of the complex, in faded blue and turquoise, and the thick brick walls with their arched niches, are plain and beautiful in the low evening light.

The riding around Navoi is flat, desert and often windy. The main highway from Samarkand to Bukhara is wide and fast, but heavily used by trucks, and the shoulders are poorly kept. Small roads lead off to villages with mulberry trees, canals and fields of cotton, and are slow but full of life. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times to ride, when the light is soft and the heat bearable, and winter, with grey skies and sometimes frost, is quiet and unglamorous.

Navoi, five and a half kilometres away, is a planned Soviet city of about 130,000 people, with fuel, shops and hotels. Near the site, there are village tea houses where you can sit and eat flat bread, grapes and cheese with strong green tea, and it is polite to take what is offered.
t.mir sayid bakhrom mausoleum@40.1,65.4:
Navoi is a strange and rather brilliant city. It does not appear on any old caravan map, because it was founded in 1958 in the middle of the Kyzylkum desert, to house the workers of the gold and uranium industries and to give the Soviet planners a clean slate. It was named after Alisher Navoi, the fifteenth-century poet who wrote in Chagatai Turkic and who has become the national literary hero. Wide avenues, tidy parks and rows of apartment blocks give it the air of a model town, and in the heat of the afternoon it is remarkably quiet.

The older story is a few kilometres away, at the Mir Sayid Bakhrom mausoleum, which lies in the village area once known as Karmana, an old trading town on the road between Samarkand and Bukhara. The mausoleum is a rare survivor from the Karakhanid period, a small, handsome building of brick with carved portals and tilework, attached to a Sufi saint of the Islamic Middle Ages. The saint's tomb is still visited and is surrounded by a grove of ancient trees, in a pleasant old cemetery. There is a pervasive feeling that this ground has been holy for a long time, and the quiet is real.

For riding, the contrast between old Karmana and new Navoi is the whole point. Navoi has broad streets that are easy to ride, with little traffic, while the roads out to the villages are narrower, with bumps, irrigation ditches and sandy shoulders. The big highway between Samarkand and Bukhara passes close by, and it is a long, straight ribbon with a heavy flow of trucks and the occasional herd of camels. Dust devils spin across the fields in summer, and winds can be strong. April and May, and the long golden autumn, are the best seasons.

Fuel, food and rooms are easy to find in Navoi, and the central bazaar sells fruit, nuts, dried apricots and flat bread. At the mausoleum, you may find a caretaker who will unlock the door and show you the interior, and you should leave a small gift. If you are travelling in summer, drink plenty of water, and wear a light scarf to cover your neck and face.
t.tashkent modernist architecture modernit:
At 5.22 in the morning on 26 April 1966, an earthquake struck the old city of Tashkent and flattened much of it. Within days, architects and engineers from across the Soviet Union arrived to rebuild, and the capital of Uzbekistan became a showcase for Soviet modernism, with wide avenues, big squares, concrete and glass blocks, and a new kind of public art. The older mud-brick lanes were largely lost, but the new architecture has a boldness of its own, now loved by a younger generation of photographers and architects.

Among the best-known buildings are the Chorsu Bazaar, with its giant green dome, and the Hotel Uzbekistan, a huge slab with a grid of windows and a mosaic frieze. The Palace of Peoples' Friendship has a sharp, theatrical outline, and the circus, shaped like a flying saucer, is a favourite of local children. The metro, opened in 1977, is a museum in itself, with each station decorated with different mosaics, chandeliers and carved marble. The Kosmonavtlar station, with its portraits of cosmonauts against a blue background, is the best known, and, once a place where photography was forbidden, it can now be photographed freely.

Tashkent is a city of about two million, flat, leafy and sprawling, with a wide road network that makes it simple to ride, but with drivers who can be erratic, and an official eye on speed limits. Wide boulevards, shaded by plane trees, run in straight lines, and the traffic can be heavy at rush hour. Lanes are sometimes ignored, and trams and buses often stop without warning, so ride defensively. Fuel can occasionally be limited, since many vehicles run on compressed natural gas, so check that your bike's fuel is available at the stations you pass. The best seasons are April to June and September to October, since summers are very hot and winters can be cold and grey.

Outside the city, the Chimgan mountains, about ninety kilometres away, offer cool air and views of the western Tian Shan, and the road there climbs through orchards and foothills. Back in town, try plov, the national dish of rice, lamb and carrots, served at midday in huge cauldrons, and take a flat bread warm from a clay oven.
t.aksu jabagly state nature reserve karaba:
Tulips grow wild in the western Tien Shan, and this is where they come from. In April and early May, the foothills of the Talas Alatau, in southern Kazakhstan, turn red, yellow and white with several species of wild tulip, including Greig's tulip, which gave rise to many garden varieties. The Aksu-Jabagly State Nature Reserve, founded in 1926, is the oldest in Central Asia, and it protects a section of this range, from steppe foothills to snowy peaks over four thousand metres.

Karabastau is one of the entry points to the reserve, a gorge where the Aksu river emerges from the mountains. Some twenty-five kilometres from the nearest village, Bayzhansay, it is a place of cliffs, juniper woods and meadows, and rock carvings of animals, hunters and symbols, some thousands of years old, can be found in the nearby canyon. The reserve shelters argali, ibex and brown bears, with snow leopards in the high country, and birds such as the lammergeier soar above the cliffs. It forms part of the Western Tien-Shan, a UNESCO site since 2016.

Access is controlled. The reserve and the border zone beyond it require permits, which you usually arrange in advance through the reserve office, and rangers at the entrance check them. The tracks are rough, with fords and stones, and are best taken on a light bike or in a hired jeep with a driver who knows the water levels. Spring floods and summer storms can wash out the road, and snow closes it in winter. Take extra fuel, tools and plenty of water.

Fuel and food are not available at the gorge. The nearest reliable places lie a long way off, and the big city of Shymkent has everything. Local families in Bayzhansay sometimes offer simple meals of bread, tea, cheese and mutton soup. Carry what you need and be self-sufficient.

April, when the tulips are out and the snow still lies on the peaks, is the moment to come.
t.karachi@24.9,67.0:
Karachi is one of the largest cities on Earth, and it behaves like it. More than eleven million people live here, by the official count, and the real number is probably higher, in a sprawl along the Arabian Sea that never really stops. The traffic is a wall of buses, rickshaws, motorbikes, donkey carts and overloaded trucks, and the air smells of diesel, frying oil and sea.

It is also surprisingly layered. The old British colonial centre has Gothic and Mughal-revival buildings like Frere Hall and the Mohatta Palace, a pink sandstone mansion from the 1920s, now a museum. The Mausoleum of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, a white marble cube, stands on a hill in the city and draws visitors from around the country. The beaches at Clifton, with camel rides and food stalls, fill up on Sunday evenings. Karachi is the commercial and financial heart of Pakistan, and the port handles most of the country's trade. The food, from spicy biryani to nihari and sweet lassi, is excellent, and cheap.

For a rider the city is something to leave, and the best way is early. The Makran Coastal Highway, the N-10, starts on the western side near the Hub River and runs about 650 kilometres along the Balochistan coast to Gwadar, through desert, mountains and sea cliffs. You pass through the sprawl of the city first, and rush-hour traffic can add hours. Once out, the road is a good-quality highway with long straights and a few bends, with sea views, strange eroded rock formations and almost no traffic.

Practical matters are important. Fuel is plentiful in Karachi, and you should fill every container you have, since stations on the coast are far apart. Carry water, and carry food. Security checkpoints are common in Balochistan, and you should carry identification, and check current local advice and any permission requirements before you travel. Summers are searing, with temperatures above forty degrees, so go in the cooler months of November to March.

Start at dawn, and eat a proper breakfast of paratha and chai before you go. The city will wake behind you, and the desert will open ahead.
t.deggaron mosque@40.2,65.0:
In the village of Hazara, in the Zarafshan valley between Bukhara and Samarkand, stands one of the oldest mosques in Central Asia. The Deggaron mosque dates from the eleventh century, and from the outside it looks almost humble: a square, squat brick building with a cluster of low domes. Inside, it is a revelation, with massive brick columns supporting a forest of small domes and arches, the brickwork laid in patterns that play with light and shadow. It is a rare survivor of the pre-Mongol architecture of the region, and it forms part of the Silk Roads listing for the Zarafshan-Karakum corridor, inscribed by UNESCO in 2023.

The Zarafshan, whose name means gold-strewing, brings meltwater from the Pamir-Alay mountains down into the desert, and for thousands of years its valley has been a ribbon of green, fields, orchards and mulberry trees, between the sands. Caravans of the Silk Road moved along it, linking Samarkand and Bukhara, and the region is dotted with ruined caravanserais, fortresses and settlements. Today cotton and wheat grow in the fields, and villages of mud-brick houses with flat roofs line the canals.

Riding in Uzbekistan is an adventure. The main road between Samarkand and Bukhara is generally decent, but it can be rough in places, and the traffic, a mix of old Soviet cars, buses, trucks and donkey carts, demands attention. Police checkpoints are common, so carry your documents. The landscape is flat and open, with long straight roads and wide horizons, and July heat on the open plain is brutal, so April, May and October suit a ride far better. Side roads to the villages are narrow and sometimes unpaved.

Fuel can be a challenge: many Uzbek cars run on compressed gas, and petrol stations, especially for higher octane fuel, can be scarce outside the cities, so fill up whenever you can. Qiziltepa and Navoi are the nearest towns, and Bukhara and Samarkand have everything. Uzbek hospitality is warm, and the food, plov, samsa and grilled shashlik with fresh flatbread, is hearty. Dress modestly when visiting the mosque, and ask before taking photographs inside.
t.rabati malik caravanserai@40.1,65.1:
Only the portal of Rabati Malik is left standing, but what a portal it is: a tall brick façade with a great arch, framed by fluted columns and decorated with intricate brick patterns, rising beside the road between Bukhara and Samarkand in the steppe of central Uzbekistan. It was built in the eleventh century by the Karakhanid rulers as a royal caravanserai, a fortified palace and rest stop on the Silk Road, and travellers once found shelter, water and protection here behind its massive walls. The rest of the building was destroyed over the centuries, but archaeologists have traced its plan, and the portal itself has been restored. Across the road, a sardoba, a domed brick reservoir, collected water for the caravans and is still in good condition.

This was the main road of Transoxiana, the land beyond the Oxus, where great cities such as Bukhara and Samarkand grew rich from trade between China, Persia and the Mediterranean. Navoi, the nearest city today, is a modern industrial town named after the fifteenth-century poet Alisher Navoi, and the area around is mainly agricultural, with cotton fields, orchards and villages, with the Nuratau mountains rising to the north.

The road between Bukhara and Samarkand, which passes right by the caravanserai, is the main highway of the region and has been largely modernised, with long straight stretches across flat land and plenty of traffic, including trucks and buses. Driving in Uzbekistan can be erratic, police checkpoints are common, and speed limits are enforced with cameras. An unusual feature of the country is that many cars run on methane gas, and petrol of the higher grades can sometimes be hard to find, especially outside the cities, so fill up whenever you see a good station. The heat in summer is intense, and the best seasons for riding are spring and autumn.

Navoi, about twenty kilometres away, has fuel, hotels and restaurants, and Bukhara and Samarkand, each a couple of hours away, have everything a traveller could need and some of the most beautiful architecture in the world. Stop at a roadside chaikhana, a teahouse, for green tea, bread and a plate of plov, the national dish, and enjoy a rest on the raised wooden platforms covered with carpets, where travellers have been resting for centuries.
t.dabusiya settlement@40.0,65.8:
Halfway along the old road from Samarkand to Bukhara, where the Zeravshan valley widens into irrigated plain, there is a ruined town called Dabusiya. The Sogdians founded it, and it grew into a staging post on the Silk Road, where caravans paused for water, fodder and trade. The Arabs reached it in the early eighth century and the town held out and changed hands as the region went through conquest and conversion. By the Middle Ages it was a modest brick town with a citadel, a mosque and workshops. The Mongols and later shifts in the river sealed its decline.

The remains today are fragments of fortification, low earthen swells and the outlines of streets, set among cotton, wheat and melon fields. It is the kind of site where the history is mostly imagined from the shape of the ground, and nothing prepares you for the quiet. There is a small area of signboards but little in the way of facilities, so the visit is short and thoughtful, with the rest of the time given to the road.

The road is what this stop is really about. The highway between Samarkand and Bukhara runs across a flat, dry steppe plain of about two hundred and fifty kilometres, and it is straightforward but demanding in its own way. Surfaces vary between smooth modern asphalt and broken sections with potholes, trucks move in convoys, and heat in summer reaches the forties, with strong sun and long distances between shade. Spring brings green fields and poppies, autumn is warm and golden, and winter can bring fog.

Yangirabot, about seventeen kilometres away, is a town of some size, and it is the sensible place for fuel, bread and a meal. Beyond it, small roadside cafés and chaikhanas, tea houses, serve lamb kebab, plov and green tea at wooden platforms called tapchans, where you can take off your boots and lie down in the shade. Fuel can be hard to come by in Uzbekistan, with shortages of petrol at times, so fill up whenever you can and carry a reserve. Bring plenty of water, wear sunscreen, and leave early to get the best of the day.
t.central exhibition hall of the academy o:
On April 26, 1966, an earthquake flattened much of old Tashkent, leaving tens of thousands homeless, and the Soviet Union responded by turning the city into a showcase. Architects and builders came from across the republics to rebuild, and the result was a capital of wide avenues, big squares and concrete modernism, with buildings that mixed Soviet geometry with Central Asian patterns, blue tiles, carved screens and domes. The Central Exhibition Hall of the Academy of Arts belongs to that world, a hall for displays of painting and sculpture, standing in a city that has since added glass towers and new mosques but keeps these older shapes as part of its character.

Tashkent is a city of about two million, built on a flat plain where the Chirchik river comes down out of the Tien Shan mountains, and it is much greener than first impressions suggest, with plane trees, canals and shaded parks. Once the Russian colonial capital of Turkestan, it became the fourth biggest city of the Soviet Union, and it still has the broad, orderly grid of a planned city. Underneath the modern surface lies the old quarter, a maze of low mud-brick houses and courtyards near Chorsu, where people still live in the traditional way.

For a rider, this is a start and finish point, a place for a hotel and a restaurant before the mountains. City traffic is dense and quick, lanes are suggestions, and drivers do not always signal, so ride defensively and expect police checks. Petrol availability has been uneven in Uzbekistan for some years, with many vehicles running on compressed gas, so check where you can fill up before a long leg, and carry a little extra. The ride from here goes to Besh-Aral, a state nature reserve, on the roads that head out across the steppe and desert fringe, with long views and little traffic outside the towns.

The best time for riding is spring, in April and May, when the steppe is green, and autumn, in September and October, when the heat has gone. Summer in Tashkent is very hot, with temperatures that often pass forty degrees, and winters can be cold and grey. In the evenings, the cafes serve plov, the rice and meat pilaf that is the national dish, with flat bread, green tea and sweet melons. Take time for a walk through the city's metro, which is a remarkable underground gallery, and where rules on photography have recently relaxed.
t.peoples friendship palace@41.3,69.2:
The Palace of Peoples' Friendship is a Soviet-era building of Tashkent that rewards a slow look, and the name itself is a period piece. Friendship of the peoples was a standard phrase of Soviet ideology, a promise that the many nationalities of the union lived in harmony, and Tashkent, with its mix of Uzbeks, Russians, Tatars, Koreans and others, was held up as the model of it. The palace, a large concert and congress hall in the modernist style, carries the ambitions of the 1960s and 1970s, when the earthquake rebuilding turned the city into a laboratory of Soviet design, and the structure stands out among the plane trees with its confident, geometric form.

Behind the heroic phrases is a real story. After the 1966 earthquake, the Soviet republics each sent teams to rebuild a district, and Tashkent became a kind of showcase of what the union could do. In the same period, the Tashkent metro, the first in Central Asia, opened in 1977, with stations decorated in tiles, carved marble and ornamental plaster, and the city grew into a major industrial and scientific centre, home to film studios and a famous film festival. The city also took in huge numbers of evacuees during the Second World War, and many people still speak of its generosity.

The ride from here goes to the Chatkal State Biosphere Reserve, in the western Tien Shan, northeast of the city, and the road out is a pleasure after the urban sprawl. It leads past Gazalkent and along the shores of Charvak reservoir, a long turquoise lake in the mountains, with smooth tarmac, gentle bends and fine views of snowy peaks. At the weekend, the road is busy with city people heading for the lake, the hills and the ski resort of Chimgan, so go early on a weekday for the quietest ride. The reserve itself protects juniper forests, walnut groves, alpine meadows and a population of bears, ibex and, high up, snow leopards.

Tashkent offers every service you need, with fuel stations on the ring road, though availability of petrol varies, so check ahead and keep your tank full. Food is plentiful and cheap: samsa baked in clay ovens, grilled lamb skewers, and bowls of cold sour milk drinks in the summer heat. April to June and September to October are the best months for the mountain roads, with a cool, bright light on the snow.
t.alisher navoi cinema palace@41.3,69.3:
Alisher Navoi never saw Tashkent, or at least no record says he did, yet his name hangs over half the city. Born in Herat in 1441, a courtier and poet at the Timurid court, he argued passionately that Turkic could be as fine a literary language as Persian, and he wrote a vast body of verse and prose in the Chagatai Turkic that Uzbeks consider the ancestor of their own tongue. Streets, a theatre, a library and a national park carry his name, and so does this cinema palace, a monument to the idea that a city should have a hall of dreams named after its poet.

Cinema was serious business in Soviet Tashkent. The city had its own film studio, which turned out comedies, historical epics and the odd adventure film set on the steppe, and it hosted a festival of Asian and African films that drew directors from across the world. The cinema palace belongs to that culture of big, public places for entertainment, where families dressed up for an evening show. The building stands in a city that was reshaped after the 1966 earthquake, with wide boulevards, fountains and a taste for large, symmetrical forms.

Your day on the bike heads north-east, away from the capital, to the Chatkal range on the border with Kyrgyzstan. The road leaves the suburbs, runs through orchards and along the Chirchik river, then climbs into the foothills, where the air cools and the villages cluster on the slopes. The mountains of the western Tien Shan stand up like a wall, with snow on the peaks until early summer, and the valleys are full of walnut and apple trees. The road is smooth in places and patched in others, and in spring, rockfalls and mud can slip onto the asphalt. Bring warm clothes: even in July, the passes are cold in the evening.

In the city, the usual rules apply. Traffic is fast, lane discipline is loose, and police stand at many junctions, sometimes waving riders aside for document checks, so keep your papers and licence handy. Petrol is not always on sale at every station, and many cars run on gas, so do not let your tank run low, and fill up before leaving town. Food is easy to find: plov at lunchtime, kebabs in the evening, and fresh bread from a clay oven, with green tea poured into small bowls. The best seasons for the mountain ride are May, June and September.
t.state museum of arts@41.3,69.3:
The best Orientalist painter of Turkestan was a Russian who hated war. Vasily Vereshchagin came to Tashkent in the 1860s as an artist attached to the Russian army, and he painted the bazaars, the beggars and the mosques of Central Asia with a precision that shocked his patrons, and then went on to paint scenes of battle that showed the dead as they were. His canvases are among the treasures of Russian art, and their subject was the world that lies around Tashkent today. The State Museum of Arts of Uzbekistan holds paintings of this kind, along with works by Russian and European artists, and a good collection of Uzbek applied art.

Applied art is the strong suit of the region. Look for suzani, the large embroidered hangings with bold flower and sun designs that brides once stitched as part of their dowry, ceramics glazed in the deep blues and greens of Samarkand and Bukhara, carved wooden doors and columns, and ikat silk, with its blurred, feathery patterns. These are crafts that survived through the Soviet years in family workshops and have since been revived. The museum is one of the best places in Tashkent to see them in one place.

The ride from the museum goes to Besh-Aral, a state nature reserve, across the plain beyond the city, and it is a very different kind of day. The roads leave the city and run through cotton fields and orchards, with canals and rows of poplars, and the horizon opens out. Traffic thins quickly after the suburbs, though lorries and buses keep to the main routes, and you should expect to be stopped at the occasional checkpoint. The surface can be uneven, and drivers often overtake with little warning, so it pays to stay alert and keep to a steady pace. The wind can pick up in the afternoon, bringing dust.

Tashkent has fuel stations, but petrol is not always available, so check and plan, and carry a small reserve. In the heat of summer, temperatures can exceed forty degrees, and the best months are April, May, September and October. Dress in layers, and carry water, a hat and sunscreen. At the end of the day, a table at a courtyard restaurant with a plate of grilled lamb, tomato and onion salad, flat bread and a pot of tea is a good reward, and the cool of the evening is a pleasure after the sun.
t.kosmonavtlar metro station@41.3,69.3:
On the Tashkent metro, the stations are the sights. The system opened in 1977, the first in Central Asia, and the Soviet planners treated each stop as a small palace, with a theme, a colour scheme and local craftsmen to carry it out. Marble, carved alabaster, mosaics and chandeliers decorate the platforms, and the Kosmonavtlar station, the Cosmonauts, is one of the best, with a space theme: blue-grey tiles, circular lamps like planets and portraits of cosmonauts, a tribute to the space programme of which Uzbekistan was proud. For years, photography underground was banned, and the rule has now relaxed, so you can look around with a camera if you are polite.

The metro is also a way to feel the Soviet dream of Tashkent as a modern, socialist city. After the 1966 earthquake, the capital was rebuilt as a showpiece of the Soviet east, with wide avenues, fountains and big public spaces, and the metro was the crowning piece, a clean, cheap, efficient system that ran on time. Today it still carries hundreds of thousands of people a day, and it remains one of the best ways to cross the city.

The ride from here points to the mountains again, to the Chatkal Biosphere Reserve in the western Tien Shan. Take the road along the Chirchik river to Gazalkent, and on into the valleys of the Pskem and Ugam, where the roads become narrower, the air cooler, and the forests of walnut and juniper thicken. The peaks reach well over three thousand metres, and in spring they are streaked with snow. The tarmac is generally decent, with some rough sections, rockfalls and sudden bends, and the valleys can be misty in the morning. Check whether permits are needed near the border with Kyrgyzstan, as some zones are restricted.

Tashkent has fuel and workshops, but petrol supplies can be uneven, so fill up early and carry a little extra. There are small cafes along the road to the mountains serving shashlik and fresh bread, and many people sell apples, apricots or honey by the roadside. Mid-May to June is a fine time for the ride, with green slopes and fresh flowers, and September brings a clear, golden light and the walnut harvest.
t.zhemchug residential building@41.3,69.3:
Zhemchug means pearl in Russian, and it is the name given to a residential building in Tashkent that looks nothing like an ordinary apartment block. In the years after the 1966 earthquake, when the city was rebuilt, Soviet architects used housing as a stage for their ideas, and some of the results are strange and rather wonderful: curved facades, great circular forms, concrete screens that echo Islamic patterns, and apartments arranged around internal courtyards. The Pearl is one of the well-known examples, and photographers of Soviet modernism have made it a favourite subject.

Housing in Tashkent has a social history that is worth knowing. The traditional unit of life was the mahalla, a neighbourhood of low houses around a shared courtyard, with a council of elders, a tea house and a mosque, and in the Soviet years many of these were demolished to make room for blocks and boulevards. Others survived, and they still give the old city its human scale. After the earthquake, the new districts were built with the help of republics from across the union, and each had a different character. Today, the tension between the old courtyards and the new towers is still part of the city's mood.

Riding out of Tashkent toward the Chatkal reserve is quite an experience, and it begins with the Ring Road and then the long road north-east along the river. The first stretch is busy, with shared taxis and lorries, and the lanes are narrow. After Gazalkent, the traffic thins, and the valley closes in, with orchards, walnut groves and the mountain walls rising on either side. The air is clearer and cooler, and the road gets better the higher you go. In summer, the mountains are an escape from the heat of the plain, and in spring, the slopes are bright with tulips.

Fuel can be a puzzle in Uzbekistan, as many cars use gas, and some stations only sell it, so look for a petrol pump before you leave and fill up whenever you can. Tashkent also has the best choice of food and hotels in the country, with a vast market and cafes at every corner. Try the thick, hot noodle soup called lagman, and the warm flat breads that are baked in clay ovens and stacked on market stalls. Be prepared for police stops, which are routine, and keep your documents ready.
t.state museum of history@41.3,69.3:
Long before Tashkent became a Soviet showpiece, it was a stop on the caravan road, and the State Museum of History tries to tell that long story. Under the name Chach, the oasis was known to the ancient Persians and Greeks, and later to Chinese travellers, who called it Shi. It lay on the Silk Road, on the route that led from Samarkand across the Syr Darya into the Fergana valley and the Chinese lands beyond. Sogdian merchants carried silk, glass, metalwork and religious ideas along it, and the museum's collections include coins, ceramics, carved stone and remains from sites across Uzbekistan, from the Bronze Age to the Timurid empire.

The great figure of the later period was Amir Timur, the conqueror known in the West as Tamerlane, who built his capital at Samarkand in the late fourteenth century and filled it with domes of blue tile, and whose name is now a symbol of national pride in Uzbekistan. His grandson Ulugh Beg, the astronomer, built an observatory there, and his star catalogue was famous across the world. The museum also covers the Russian conquest in the nineteenth century, when Tashkent was taken in 1865 and became the capital of Russian Turkestan, and the Soviet period that followed.

For a rider, the museum is a good morning stop before the day's drive to the Chatkal Biosphere Reserve, to the north-east. The road follows the Chirchik river out of the city, with views of cotton fields and orchards, and then enters the mountain foothills, where the walnut forests begin. The reserve covers peaks, juniper woods and meadows, and the trails are best done on foot, with a local guide. The roads in the mountains vary, with smooth sections, and some broken surface, and hairpin bends on the steeper climbs. Rain can bring stones down, so keep your speed measured.

Tashkent has the best range of services, with fuel stations, mechanics, and shops, though petrol is not always on sale, and gas is common, so check before you rely on a station. The nearby parks offer shade in summer, when the heat is intense. Try fresh fruit from the markets, such as apricots and melons, which are sweet and cheap in season, and fill your water bottle before leaving. Autumn is mild and clear, with a good light for the mountains.
t.chorsu market@41.3,69.2:
The blue dome of Chorsu is the best landmark in old Tashkent. The great market under it, a huge circular hall roofed with a single sky-blue cupola, stands on the site of a crossroads whose name means four streams or four roads, and the bazaar here has been the heart of the old city for centuries, long before the Soviet engineers built the dome. Around it, in the surrounding lanes, stalls spill into the streets, and the noise, smell and colour are overwhelming: pyramids of spice, mounds of dried apricots, raisins and nuts, piles of round, patterned breads, hanging carcasses at the butchers' hall, and women in bright dresses calling out prices.

The place rewards slow wandering. The bread sellers stack their loaves, called non, with stamped patterns in the centre, in towering piles, and each region has its own style. The spice merchants offer saffron, cumin, dried barberries for plov, and heaps of red pepper, and the dairy sellers offer balls of dried salty yoghurt, called qurt. Samsa, the baked pastries filled with lamb, are sold hot from the clay ovens, and you eat them standing up, with a paper napkin, in the steam. In late summer, melons, grapes and pomegranates arrive from the Fergana valley.

The ride that starts here goes out to the Besh-Aral reserve beyond the plain, and the market is a good place to buy supplies, such as bread, dried fruit and nuts, and a bottle of water. Getting out of Tashkent takes some patience, with traffic that is fast and loose, and the market area is crowded, with narrow streets and many pedestrians, so park your bike carefully in a guarded place and walk. Once you leave the suburbs, the roads open up across the steppe and cotton fields, with long straight stretches, and some rough patches.

Petrol is not guaranteed, because supplies in Uzbekistan can be erratic and many vehicles run on gas, so check and fill up early. The best seasons for riding are April to June and September to October. At midday in summer the heat is brutal, so plan to be on the road early. Visit the market in the morning, when it is busiest and freshest, and leave the afternoon for the road.
t.state circus@41.3,69.2:
The Tashkent circus looks like a landed spaceship, or a giant pale flying saucer, and for decades it was one of the city's proudest buildings. Circus was a serious art form in the Soviet Union, with its own schools, state companies and international stars, and every large city had a permanent big top made of concrete. The one in Tashkent, a round building with a huge dome, was built in the 1970s and holds nearly two thousand spectators, and the tradition of acrobats, trained animals, clowns and trapeze artists is a cherished part of the city's culture, with many families bringing their children on Sundays.

The building belongs to the era of reconstruction after the 1966 earthquake, when the city was given large public monuments of concrete and tile, in forms that were meant to look to the future. Many have weathered the changes since independence, and some have been restored, while others face an uncertain fate. It is worth a look from the outside, at least, as an example of a particular, optimistic kind of architecture.

For a day on the bike, the circus is a convenient starting point, in the middle of the capital, for the road toward the Chatkal Biosphere Reserve, in the western Tien Shan. The way out leads north-east through the suburbs and along the river, then into orchards and villages, and the valleys narrow as the mountains close in. The surface is mostly good, but watch for potholes and for slow trucks on the climbs. In late spring, the hills glow green, and the cherry and apricot trees bloom in the foothill villages, while in summer the mountains give a cool break from the heat of the city.

Tashkent has plenty of fuel stations, though petrol is not always available, so do not let the tank run low, and fill up before you leave. Eating is easy, with kebabs, plov and fresh bread on offer at every corner, and green tea. Remember that police checkpoints are common, and keep your documents at hand. The best months for the ride are May, June and September, with temperatures that are pleasant and views that are clear, and avoid the hottest weeks of July and August.
t.tashkent@41.3,69.2:
Tashkent is the capital of Uzbekistan and the big, green, slightly surprising gateway to the Silk Road. It is a city of two million people with wide avenues, shady plane trees, fountains and a good deal of Soviet architecture, because a catastrophic earthquake in 1966 flattened much of the old town and the whole republic helped to rebuild it. What survived is mostly in the old quarter, around the Chorsu bazaar, with its blue-domed hall, spice stalls and mountains of bread, nuts and dried fruit.

As a start point for a long ride south-west towards Samarkand and Bukhara, it works well, although getting out is the usual big-city chore. Traffic is dense and quick, lane discipline is a suggestion, and cars cut in with little warning. Leave early, ideally before eight, and use the main road out towards Samarkand, which is wide and fairly fast. Summer is hot, regularly above thirty-five degrees by midday, so spring and early autumn are much kinder. Winter can be cold and grey. Road surfaces on the main highways are generally good, though patches and sudden potholes appear, and police posts along the route are common, so keep your documents handy.

Worth a look before you set off is the metro, which many people regard as one of the finest in the former Soviet Union, with stations decorated like palaces in marble, chandeliers and mosaics. Amir Timur Square, with its statue of the conqueror who made Samarkand his capital, gives a sense of the national story, and the old Khast Imam complex holds one of the oldest Qurans in the world, the Uthman Quran. For food, plov is the answer: a pilaf of rice, carrot and meat cooked in a huge cauldron, served at lunch time and often sold out by two. Fresh flatbread, samsa and green tea come with everything.

On practical matters, Tashkent has no shortage of anything, including repair shops and stations. Fuel supply outside the capital can vary, with some forecourts selling gas rather than petrol, so fill the tank when you can and check before long stretches. Carry some local cash, because card use is spotty outside the city.
t.turkistan@43.3,68.3:
Turkistan is the spiritual centre of Kazakhstan, a city of nearly a hundred thousand people in the hot, flat south, built around one great building. The Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, a twelfth-century Sufi poet and teacher whose ideas helped spread Islam among the Turkic nomads, rises from the middle of town with a huge blue-glazed dome and a portal covered in tilework. Timur ordered it built in the late fourteenth century, and it was never entirely finished, which gives its rough brick back a curious, unfinished honesty. It is a UNESCO site, and it is a pilgrimage destination for Kazakhs who consider three visits equal to one trip to Mecca.

Around the mausoleum, modern Turkistan has been given an enthusiastic makeover, with wide avenues, new museums, a large park and a rebuilt citadel. For several centuries the city was a political centre as well, a capital of the Kazakh khanate in the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, and it stood on a branch of the Silk Road where caravans paused before heading east or west. The older quarter has fragments of walls, bathhouses and a museum with finds from digs in the region.

For a rider, the approach is a long, mostly straight run across steppe, with dry grass, scattered villages, irrigated fields and big trucks. It is not a technical ride, and the heat is the main challenge, with summer temperatures that can climb beyond forty degrees. Spring and autumn are far more comfortable, and early morning or evening is the best time to be on the road. Watch for livestock, patchy surfaces and drivers who overtake when they should not. Wind can blow hard across the plain.

As a stop, Turkistan has everything. It is large enough for fuel, hotels, supermarkets, cafes and spare-part shops, and it is a reasonable base for exploring the nearby ruined cities of Sauran and Otrar. Try the local bread, beshbarmak, a dish of boiled meat and noodles, and strong tea with plenty of sugar. In the evenings, when the heat eases and the mausoleum is lit, local families stroll across the plaza and the whole place has a festive feel.
t.sauran@43.5,68.3:
Sauran is a city that has mostly turned into mounds, but what mounds. On the steppe northwest of Turkistan, not far from Kentau, the ruins of a medieval walled town rise from the plain, with long lines of mud-brick fortifications, bastions and gates still tracing a shape that can be read from a distance. For centuries this was one of the important towns on the northern branch of the Silk Road, a market and a fortress on the edge of the nomad world, and it changed hands between powers that wanted its walls.

In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries it became a significant point in struggles between Timurid, Shaybanid and Kazakh forces, and by the sixteenth century it was a centre of the Kazakh khanate. Then trade shifted, wars wore it down, and by the eighteenth century it was abandoned. Archaeologists have uncovered streets, houses, a bathhouse and a sophisticated water system, and the scale of the walls shows how seriously people took defence. Today the site is a quiet open-air museum, and you are likely to have it largely to yourself.

The ride out is a short drive from Turkistan and Kentau on mostly paved roads, followed by a short stretch of rougher track, so check conditions after rain, when the clay turns slippery. It is dry, wide-open steppe, with grass, thorny shrubs and the occasional shepherd or herd of horses. Wind and sun are the main discomforts, and there is little shade, so bring a hat, water and sunscreen. Spring, when the grass is green and flowers scatter the plain, is easily the nicest time.

You will not find fuel or food at the site itself, so refill in Turkistan or Kentau, and carry a snack. Walk the wall for a few minutes and look out across the steppe: it is not hard to imagine caravans arriving at dusk, the gate closing behind them. The mud brick is fragile, so be careful where you step and leave stones where they lie. It is a modest stop with an enormous sense of time.
t.otrar@42.9,68.3:
Otrar is where a single diplomatic disaster helped change the history of Asia. In 1218, the governor of this city, an official of the Khwarezmian empire, seized a trade caravan sent by Genghis Khan and executed its merchants, and when the Mongol ruler's envoys protested, one of them was killed too. The Mongols responded with a campaign that destroyed Khwarezm and, in time, much of Central Asia. Otrar was besieged and sacked, and its governor reportedly met a grim end.

The city stood where the Arys river met the Syr Darya, in a fertile belt of irrigated land, and it was a major stop on the Silk Road long before the Mongols. It was also the birthplace of Al-Farabi, the tenth-century philosopher and scholar often called the Second Teacher after Aristotle, and it was where Timur died in 1405, while leading an army toward China. Today the site, called Otrar-Tobe, is a large mound with fragments of walls, streets and a citadel, standing in flat, open farmland.

The ride from Turkistan is straightforward: paved roads across the plain, passing the small village of Qogham, with the occasional pothole and plenty of livestock. The landscape is flat, hot and dry in summer, with fields and canals around the river, and vivid green in spring. It is easy riding, but also demanding in its own way, with long straight sections that can lull you, side winds, and heat. Early morning or evening makes the most sense, and a good hat is better than any fashion.

Fuel and food are not available at the site, and Qogham is a small village, so arrive with a full tank from Turkistan, which has all the services you need. A small museum nearby displays finds from the excavations, and the visit takes an hour or two. There is little shade and no great spectacle, only broken walls and a sense of scale, so it appeals most to people who like history. Bring water, take your time, and perhaps stand on the mound at sunset, when the dust turns the light gold and the ruin looks as it did to the last caravan.
t.shymkent@42.3,69.6:
Shymkent is the big, hot, unpretentious city of the south. With more than four hundred thousand people, it is the third largest city in Kazakhstan and, since a reform a few years ago, administered separately from the surrounding region. It lies close to the Uzbek border, in a green, irrigated plain below the western Tian Shan, and it feels different from the rest of the country: more Silk Road bazaar than steppe outpost, with a mix of Kazakh, Uzbek, Russian and other communities and a food scene to match. The name is often connected with a word for a green place, which suits an oasis.

The city is old, though it hides it well. A caravan settlement stood here for many centuries, and the nearby town of Sayram, now a suburb of sorts, was a major Silk Road stop with a history reaching back more than a thousand years. Shymkent's modern look comes largely from Soviet planning, with wide avenues, plane trees, parks and apartment blocks, softened by a busy, chatty street life. The central bazaar is worth an hour, with piles of dried fruit, nuts, spices, bread, melons and tea.

The riding into and around the city is straightforward: roads are wide and traffic is brisk, with a noticeable disregard for lanes. Rush hours are slow, and in summer the heat is intense, easily above thirty-five degrees by midday and sometimes much higher. Ride early, drink water and treat the afternoon as siesta time. Spring and autumn are lovely, and the foothills to the east catch some rain and are covered with green and flowers for a short season.

This is a place to do all the dull and essential things. Fuel is easy to find, repair shops and parts dealers exist in numbers, and there are plenty of hotels in every price range. Eat plov, samsa, manty and shashlik, and drink tea in the shade of a courtyard. It makes a sensible base before heading east toward the mountains of Aksu-Zhabagly, or west and north toward Turkistan. Treat it as a hub, enjoy the food, and leave with a full tank.
